avail.e: From Middle English availen (“to be of use”), from Old French a (“to”) + vail from valoir (“to be worth”), from Latin valere (“to be worthy, strong”).
avail.g: To turn to the advantage of.

available.e: From Middle English available, avayllable, avayleable, equivalent of avail + -able.
available.g: Such as one may avail oneself of; capable of being used for the accomplishment of a purpose.

aven.g: A vertical shaft leading upward from a cave passage, sometimes connecting with passages above.

avenge.e: From Middle English avengen, borrowed from Old French avengier, from a- + vengier.
avenge.g: To take vengeance (for); to exact satisfaction for by punishing the injuring party; to vindicate by inflicting pain or evil on a wrongdoer.

avenger.e: From Middle English avengere; equivalent to avenge + -er.

averse.e: From Latin aversus, past participle of avertere (“to avert”).
averse.g: Having a repugnance or opposition of mind.

avert.e: From Middle English averten, adverten, from Old French avertir (“turn, direct, avert; turn the attention, make aware”), from Latin āvertere, from ab + vertō (“to turn”).

avoid.e: From Middle English avoiden, from Anglo-Norman avoider, Old French esvuidier (“to empty out”), from es- + vuidier, from Vulgar Latin *vocitāre < Vulgar Latin *vocitum, ultimately related to Latin vacuus.
avoid.g: To try not to meet or communicate with (a person); to shun.

avouch.e: From Old French avouchier, from Latin advocāre.
avouch.g: To declare freely and openly; to assert.
